title: Product Measures and Fubini-Tonelli Theorems

html:
In this post we collect standard materials on product measures, including a description for the Komolgorov's extension theorem. There are two pillars under the theory: the monotone convergence theorem, which is already important in developing the Lebesgue integration theory, and the monotone class lemma, which can be viewed as a set-theoretic counterpart of the former. Putting them together implies the all-important Fubini-Tonelli theorems that allow one to compute integrals, reducing higher dimensions to lower ones, leading also to tricks to calculating integrals such as the Gaussians. I have followed the Terry's notes most of the time.

1.1. Finite product measure spaces

The cartesian product X×Y {X\times Y}X×Y of two sets X {X}X and Y {Y}Y is characterized by the associated projection maps

πX:X×Y→XπY:X×Y→Y.\displaystyle \pi_{X}:X\times Y\rightarrow X\quad\pi_{Y}:X\times Y\rightarrow Y.πX​:X×Y→XπY​:X×Y→Y.

We can make use of these maps to construct a product σ {\sigma}σ-algebra: given two measurable spaces (X,BX) {(X,\mathcal{B}_{X})}(X,BX​) and (Y,BY) {(Y,\mathcal{B}_{Y})}(Y,BY​), we can form a collections of subsets in X×Y {X\times Y}X×Y by pulling back BX {\mathcal{B}_{X}}BX​:

πX∗(BX):={πX−1(E):E∈BX}={E×Y:E∈BX}.\displaystyle \pi_{X}^{*}(\mathcal{B}_{X}):=\{\pi_{X}^{-1}(E):E\in\mathcal{B}_{X}\}=\{E\times Y:E\in\mathcal{B}_{X}\}.πX∗​(BX​):={πX−1​(E):E∈BX​}={E×Y:E∈BX​}.

It is easily verifyed that πX∗(BX) {\pi_{X}^{*}(\mathcal{B}_{X})}πX∗​(BX​) is a σ {\sigma}σ-algebra. Note that ∅×Y=∅ {\emptyset\times Y=\emptyset}∅×Y=∅.

Definition 1 (Finite product σ {\sigma}σ-algebra) The product σ {\sigma}σ-algebra BX×BY {\mathcal{B}_{X}\times\mathcal{B}_{Y}}BX​×BY​ is defined to be the σ {\sigma}σ-algebra generated by the union of the pullback σ {\sigma}σ-algebras

BX×BY=⟨πX∗(BX)∪πY∗(BY)⟩.\displaystyle \mathcal{B}_{X}\times\mathcal{B}_{Y}=\langle\pi_{X}^{*}(\mathcal{B}_{X})\cup\pi_{Y}^{*}(\mathcal{B}_{Y})\rangle.BX​×BY​=⟨πX∗​(BX​)∪πY∗​(BY​)⟩.

By observing that E×Y=(E×Y)∪∅ {E\times Y=(E\times Y)\cup\emptyset}E×Y=(E×Y)∪∅, (E×Y)∩(X×F)=E×F {(E\times Y)\cap(X\times F)=E\times F}(E×Y)∩(X×F)=E×F, we see that BX×BY {\mathcal{B}_{X}\times\mathcal{B}_{Y}}BX​×BY​ is also the σ {\sigma}σ-algebra generated by rectangles E×F {E\times F}E×F, where E∈BX {E\in\mathcal{B}_{X}}E∈BX​ and F∈BY {F\in\mathcal{B}_{Y}}F∈BY​. The definition of product σ {\sigma}σ-algebra automatically makes the projection maps πX {\pi_{X}}πX​ and πY {\pi_{Y}}πY​ measurable morphisms, and in fact, it is the coarsest one that makes this happen.

Proposition 2 Let x∈X {x\in X}x∈X, y∈Y {y\in Y}y∈Y and A∈BX×BY {A\in\mathcal{B}_{X}\times\mathcal{B}_{Y}}A∈BX​×BY​. The x {x}x-slice Ax:={y:(x,y)∈A} {A_{x}:=\{y:(x,y)\in A\}}Ax​:={y:(x,y)∈A} is measurable for every x∈X {x\in X}x∈X. Similarly, the y {y}y-slice Ay:={x:(x,y)∈A} {A^{y}:=\{x:(x,y)\in A\}}Ay:={x:(x,y)∈A} is measurable for every y∈Y {y\in Y}y∈Y.

Proof: Let A {\mathcal{A}}A be the subset of BX×BY {\mathcal{B}_{X}\times\mathcal{B}_{Y}}BX​×BY​ such that Ax {A_{x}}Ax​ is measurable for all A∈A {A\in\mathcal{A}}A∈A. We are to show that A=BX×BY {\mathcal{A=\mathcal{B}_{X}\times\mathcal{B}_{Y}}}A=BX​×BY​, and it suffices to have A {\mathcal{A}}A is a σ {\sigma}σ-algebra containing all measurable rectangles.
First, since for A=E×F∈BX×BY {A=E\times F\in\mathcal{B}_{X}\times\mathcal{B}_{Y}}A=E×F∈BX​×BY​, Ax=F {A_{x}=F}Ax​=F if x∈E {x\in E}x∈E and Ax=∅ {A_{x}=\emptyset}Ax​=∅ otherwise, all measurable rectangles are contained in A {\mathcal{A}}A. So in particular X×Y∈A {X\times Y\in\mathcal{A}}X×Y∈A.
Next, if A∈A {A\in\mathcal{A}}A∈A, then (Ac)x=(Ax)c {\left(A^{c}\right)_{x}=\left(A_{x}\right)^{c}}(Ac)x​=(Ax​)c, so Ac∈A {A^{c}\in\mathcal{A}}Ac∈A. Furthermore, if Ai∈A {A_{i}\in\mathcal{A}}Ai​∈A for i=1,2,… {i=1,2,\dots}i=1,2,…, and A=⋃iAi {A=\bigcup_{i}A_{i}}A=⋃i​Ai​, then

Ax=⋃i(Ai)x\displaystyle A_{x}=\bigcup_{i}\left(A_{i}\right)_{x}Ax​=i⋃​(Ai​)x​

The converse is NOT true, as the follwing example shows.

Example 1 If B1 {\mathcal{B}_{1}}B1​, B2 {\mathcal{B}_{2}}B2​ are the Borel σ {\sigma}σ-algebras of Rd1 {\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}}Rd1​ and Rd2 {\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}}Rd2​ respectively, then B1×B2 {\mathcal{B}_{1}\times\mathcal{B}_{2}}B1​×B2​ is the Borel σ {\sigma}σ-algebra of Rd1+d2 {\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}+d_{2}}}Rd1​+d2​. This is closely related to the fact that the product topology is generated by sets of the form π1−1(U)∪π2−1(V) {\pi_{1}^{-1}(U)\cup\pi_{2}^{-1}(V)}π1−1​(U)∪π2−1​(V) for U {U}U, V {V}V open in Rd1 {\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}}Rd1​ and Rd2 {\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}}Rd2​ respectively. In contrast, the product Lebesgue σ {\sigma}σ-algebras M1×M2 {\mathcal{M}_{1}\times\mathcal{M}_{2}}M1​×M2​ on Rd1+d2 {\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}+d_{2}}}Rd1​+d2​ is not the Lebesgue σ {\sigma}σ-algebra on Rd1+d2 {\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}+d_{2}}}Rd1​+d2​. This can be seen via Proposition 2. For example, if N {\mathcal{N}}N is a non-measurable set in R {\mathbb{R}}R and E {E}E is a null set (say, a point) in R {\mathbb{R}}R, then N×E {\mathcal{N}\times E}N×E would be Lebesgue measurable in R2 {\mathbb{R}^{2}}R2, as it has measure zero.

Now, suppose we have two measure spaces (X,BX,μX) {(X,\mathcal{B}_{X},\mu_{X})}(X,BX​,μX​) and (X,BX,μX) {(X,\mathcal{B}_{X},\mu_{X})}(X,BX​,μX​). For a measurable rectangle E×F {E\times F}E×F in the product σ {\sigma}σ-algebra, we can define its measure by a product formula:

μX×μY(E×F)=μX(E)μY(F).\displaystyle \mu_{X}\times\mu_{Y}(E\times F)=\mu_{X}(E)\mu_{Y}(F).μX​×μY​(E×F)=μX​(E)μY​(F).

The question is whether we can extend it to a measure on the product σ {\sigma}σ-algebra. This will be done once we can show it is a pre-measure, since the extension will then follow from Hahn-Kolmogorov extension theorem.

Proposition 3 (Existence and uniqueness of (unsigned) product measure for σ {\sigma}σ-finite spaces) Let (X,BX,μX) {(X,\mathcal{B}_{X},\mu_{X})}(X,BX​,μX​) and (X,BX,μX) {(X,\mathcal{B}_{X},\mu_{X})}(X,BX​,μX​) be σ {\sigma}σ-finite measure spaces. Then there exists a unique measure μX×μY {\mu_{X}\times\mu_{Y}}μX​×μY​ on BX×BY {\mathcal{B}_{X}\times\mathcal{B}_{Y}}BX​×BY​ such that

μX×μY(E×F)=μX(E)μY(F)\displaystyle \mu_{X}\times\mu_{Y}(E\times F)=\mu_{X}(E)\mu_{Y}(F)μX​×μY​(E×F)=μX​(E)μY​(F)

whenever E∈BX {E\in\mathcal{B}_{X}}E∈BX​ and F∈BY {F\in\mathcal{B}_{Y}}F∈BY​.

Recall that a pre-measure μ0 {\mu_{0}}μ0​ is a set function defined on a Boolean algebra that satisfies μ0(∅)=0 {\mu_{0}(\emptyset)=0}μ0​(∅)=0, finite additivity and countable additivity on disjoint sets in the Boolean algebra. The uniqueness of the Hahn-Kolmogorov extension holds under the assumption of σ {\sigma}σ-finiteness. Note that the product measure, if exists, is σ {\sigma}σ-finite if the individual measures are σ {\sigma}σ-finite. It remains to establish the pre-measure.
Proof: Let B0 {\mathcal{B}_{0}}B0​ be the collection consists of sets of the form

S=(E1×F1)∪⋯∪(Ek×Fk)\displaystyle S=(E_{1}\times F_{1})\cup\cdots\cup(E_{k}\times F_{k})S=(E1​×F1​)∪⋯∪(Ek​×Fk​)

where Ei∈BX {E_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{X}}Ei​∈BX​, Fi∈BY {F_{i}\in\mathcal{B}_{Y}}Fi​∈BY​ for i=1,…,k {i=1,\dots,k}i=1,…,k. In other words, S {S}S is a finite union of measurable rectangles, and we shall call such sets elementary sets. Since ⋃iEi {\bigcup_{i}E_{i}}⋃i​Ei​ can be rewritten as a disjoint union ⨆iE~i {\bigsqcup_{i}\tilde{E}_{i}}⨆i​E~i​ where

E~i=(⋃j=1iEi)\⋃j=1i−1Ei,\displaystyle \tilde{E}_{i}=\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{i}E_{i}\right)\backslash\bigcup_{j=1}^{i-1}E_{i},E~i​=(j=1⋃i​Ei​)\j=1⋃i−1​Ei​,

It is also easy to see that B0 {\mathcal{B}_{0}}B0​ includes ∅ {\emptyset}∅ as an element, and is closed under complement and finite unions, thus B0 {\mathcal{B}_{0}}B0​ forms a Boolean algebra. Next, we define a function μ0:B0→[0,∞] {\mu_{0}:\mathcal{B}_{0}\rightarrow[0,\infty]}μ0​:B0​→[0,∞] by

μ0(S):=∑jμX(Ej)μY(Fj).\displaystyle \mu_{0}(S):=\sum_{j}\mu_{X}(E_{j})\mu_{Y}(F_{j}).μ0​(S):=j∑​μX​(Ej​)μY​(Fj​).

To show it is a premeasure, let S∈B0 {S\in\mathcal{B}_{0}}S∈B0​ and S1,S2,… {S_{1},S_{2},\dots}S1​,S2​,… be a countable disjoint family of elementary sets whose union is S {S}S. By the previous observation, we may assume S=E×F {S=E\times F}S=E×F, and also Sj=Ej×Fj {S_{j}=E_{j}\times F_{j}}Sj​=Ej​×Fj​ for each j {j}j. Now, because of disjointness, we have a pointwise identity

χE(x)χF(y)=∑j=1∞χEj(x)χFj(y).\displaystyle \chi_{E}(x)\chi_{F}(y)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\chi_{E_{j}}(x)\chi_{F_{j}}(y).χE​(x)χF​(y)=j=1∑∞​χEj​​(x)χFj​​(y).

∫X∑j=1∞χEj(x)χFj(y)dμY(y)=∑j=1∞∫XχEj(x)χFj(y)dμY(y)=∑j=1∞χEj(x)μY(Fj).\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} \int_{X}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\chi_{E_{j}}(x)\chi_{F_{j}}(y)d\mu_{Y}(y) & = & \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\int_{X}\chi_{E_{j}}(x)\chi_{F_{j}}(y)d\mu_{Y}(y)\\ & = & \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\chi_{E_{j}}(x)\mu_{Y}(F_{j}). \end{array}∫X​∑j=1∞​χEj​​(x)χFj​​(y)dμY​(y)​==​∑j=1∞​∫X​χEj​​(x)χFj​​(y)dμY​(y)∑j=1∞​χEj​​(x)μY​(Fj​).​

From axiom of choice, we can form

XA:=∏α∈AXα\displaystyle X_{A}:=\prod_{\alpha\in A}X_{\alpha}XA​:=α∈A∏​Xα​

for arbitrary family of sets {Xα}α∈A {\{X_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in A}}{Xα​}α∈A​, where the elements in the space are tuples xA=(xα)α∈A {x_{A}=(x_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in A}}xA​=(xα​)α∈A​. BA=∏β∈ABβ:=⟨⋃β∈Aπβ∗(Bβ)⟩.\displaystyle \mathcal{B}_{A}=\prod_{\beta\in A}\mathcal{B}_{\beta}:=\langle\bigcup_{\beta\in A}\pi_{\beta}^{*}(\mathcal{B}_{\beta})\rangle.BA​=β∈A∏​Bβ​:=⟨β∈A⋃​πβ∗​(Bβ​)⟩.

Again, it is the coarsest σ {\sigma}σ-algebra such that πβ {\pi_{\beta}}πβ​'s, and more generally πB {\pi_{B}}πB​'s are measurable morphisms. The elements in BA {\mathcal{B}_{A}}BA​, by definition of generation of σ {\sigma}σ-algebra, are formed by countable set-theoretic operations. In particular, this means that if E∈BA {E\in\mathcal{B}_{A}}E∈BA​, there exists an at most countable set B⊂A {B\subset A}B⊂A and a set EB∈BB {E_{B}\in\mathcal{B}_{B}}EB​∈BB​ such that EA=πB−1(EB) {E_{A}=\pi_{B}^{-1}(E_{B})}EA​=πB−1​(EB​). 1.3. Theorems of Fubini and Tonelli

There will be two essential tools that to establish the Fubini-type of results: one is the monotone convergence theorem, which has already played a crucial role to establish the convergence of the intetgral the proof of Proposition 2; the other is the monotone class lemma. Roughly speaking, the monotone convergence allows one to conclude convergence result in the unsigned setting, while the monotone class lemma allows one to conclude that the set, where the convergence result holds, is a σ {\sigma}σ-algebra.
We have encountered a monotone class in the very begining. A collection B {\mathcal{B}}B of subsets of X {X}X is said to be a monotone class if X {X}X satisfies the following two closure properties:

  1. If E1⊂E2⊂⋯ {E_{1}\subset E_{2}\subset\cdots}E1​⊂E2​⊂⋯ is a countable ascending sequence of sets in B {\mathcal{B}}B, then ⋃n=1∞En∈B {\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_{n}\in\mathcal{B}}⋃n=1∞​En​∈B;
  2. If E1⊃E2⊃⋯ {E_{1}\supset E_{2}\supset\cdots}E1​⊃E2​⊃⋯ is a countable descending sequence of sets in B {\mathcal{B}}B, then ⋂n=1∞En∈B {\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}E_{n}\in\mathcal{B}}⋂n=1∞​En​∈B.

Lemma 5 (Monotone class lemma) Let A {\mathcal{A}}A be a Boolean algebra on X {X}X. Then the σ {\sigma}σ-algebra generated by A {\mathcal{A}}A, denoted ⟨A⟩ {\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle}⟨A⟩ is the smallest monotone class that contains A {\mathcal{A}}A.

Proof: Obviously, ⟨A⟩ {\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle}⟨A⟩ is a monotone class.
